blocks.html: Blood Pressure

• Blood pressure (BP): the pressure exerted by blood on the wall of the blood vessels; arterial pressure in systemic circulation
  • R side = pulmonary circulation (CO2 rich, O2 poor blood); L side = systemic circulation (O2 rich, CO2 poor blood)
  • Total blood volume = 5 L; heart and pulmonary circulation = 15%, systemic arteries (distribution vessels) = 10%, systemic capillaries (exchange vessels) = 5%, systemic veins (capacitance vessels) = 70%
  • BP = systolic pressure/diastolic pressure = 120 mmHg/80 mmHg

• Low risk = 120/80, medium risk = 121-139/80-89, high risk = 140+/90
  • Physiological factors: age, gender, genetics, diet, sleep, activity, stress, hydration
  • Circulatory factors: cardiac output (heart), peripheral resistance (blood vessels)
Mean Arterial Pressure

• Mean arterial pressure (MAP): the average BP during a single cardiac cycle MAP = DP + 1/3(SP – DP) = 93 mmHg MAP = CO × TPR
  • Cardiac output (CO): the amount of blood ejected by the heart in one minute (1/min) CO = HR × SV
  • Heart rate (HR): number of contractions in 1 min
  • Stroke volume (SV): the amount of blood ejected in one contraction
  • Total peripheral resistance (TPR): the total resistance encountered by the blood from all the blood vessels

blocks.html: General Visceral Afferents and Referred Pain

• Each spinal nerve embryonically provides innervation to a single patch of skin (dermatome) and muscle (myotome), but as the embryo elongates, the patches converge, mixing nerve supply
  • Visceral sensory afferent neuron → thoracoabdominal splanchnic nerve → sympathetic chain → WRC → spinal nerve → DRG → dorsal root → dorsal grey horn → second order neuron → brain
  • Referred pain: brain is used to receiving general sensory information through the spinal cord from general sensory afferents, so it misinterprets pain from the visceral afferents as body wall pain associated with those spinal levels; diffuse, non-specific, achy
  • Pelvic pain line corresponds to the lower limit of the peritoneum
  • Follow sympathetic to T1-L3 spinal levels
  • Follow parasympathetic to S2-4 spinal levels

  • Precision: how close the data are to each other; measure of spread
  • Decision threshold: cut-off value at the upper limit of the reference range
  • Disease absent: below = true normal (TN); above = false positive (FP)
  • Disease present: below = false negative (FN); above = true positive (TP)

blocks.html:
• Screening tests are performed routinely at predetermined intervals on asymptomatic patients for early detection of disease Lowering a screening cut-point increases sensitivity but lowers specificity – SPIN SNOUT
  • Use a very sensitive test for an asymptomatic population and follow it up with a very specific test for diagnosis
  • Consider additional clinical benefit/costs of screening-informed management, “value for money”, and consequences
• Prevalence: % of patients who have the disease that is being tested; predictive value changes with disease prevalence

• Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves: false positive rate (x-axis; 1 – specificity) vs. true positive rate (y-axis; sensitivity)
  • Increased area under the curve = increased effectiveness
  • Pretest probability: likelihood a patient has the disease being tested for; higher pretest probability = higher PPV
Reference Intervals (RI)

• 95% central range of values observed in a healthy population of individuals
  • Challenging populations: pediatric, geriatric, transgender, pregnant
  • Limitations: subject demographic (age, sex, race), exclusion of 2.5% of healthy subjects on tail-ends, errors, sampling time, sample type, measurement procedures

blocks.html: Approach to Unexpected Lab Test Results

• 1. Understand the issue – not consistent with related tests/previous values for the test/presentation
  • 2. Consider pre-analytical explanations – wrong test, patient preparation, sample collection, transportation, lab processing error
  • 3. Consider analytical explanations – random error, sample mix-up by the lab, methodology difference
  • 4. Consider post-analytical explanations – transcription error, patient mix-up in reporting, inappropriate reference interval
  • 5. Consult with a lab professional – explanation, suggest other investigations/alternate methods for the test
  • 6. Consider additional testing – repeat, different analytical method, Choosing Wisely
  • 7. Consider that the result could be correct
Homeostatic Mechanisms in Response to Dehydration

• 1. Restore osmolality – hypothalamus ↑ activity of osmoreceptors, ↓ activity of stretch receptors, releases ADH
  • 2. Conserve fluid – kidneys ↑ permeability and ↓ urine output to ↑ water resorption/prevent further fluid loss
  • 3. Restore fluid volume – hypothalamus ↑ thirst
  • 4. Increase BP
  • Secretion of ADH
  • Behavioural changes
  • Changes in sodium balance
  • Cardiovascular reflexes
The Role of RAAS in Sodium Balance

• Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is activated by decreased BP and increased extracellular K+
  • Plasma osmolality > regulation of ECF volume
  • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) inhibit RAAS
Angiotensin II → ↑ aldosterone → ↑ Na+ reabsorption → vasoconstriction → ↑ ADH/thirst → ↑ ECF volume, ↑ BP, restore osmolality

blocks.html: Social Determinants of Health and Health Equity

• Life expectancy in full health in Canada: poorest fifth = 50.2 years; richest fifth = 61.4 years
  • Poorest fifth: less likely to use cancer screening services, fewer specialist visits, longer wait times, higher rates of emergency hospitalizations, avoidable deaths
  • Self-rated mental health and COPD hospitalization gaps by income have widened over time
  • Cost of health disparity in Canada = $6.1 billion
  • SDH have disproportionately affected marginalized groups during COVID-19 Chronic multimorbidities, multigeneration/dense households, work-from-home, self-isolation, rates of testing
  • Horizontal equity: equal treatment of equals in relevant respects
  • Vertical equity: unequal treatment for those who are unequal in relevant respects
Inequalities in Health Care at Key Stages of the Patient Pathway
Critical Appraisal

• Application of rules of evidence to original clinical studies to decide if the studies’ conclusions are valid and useful
  • How was the study designed? – consider screening strategies compared and the similarity of the groups at the start of the study
  • What are the results? – identify benefits (reduction of disease-specific mortality) and potential harms Lead-time bias: occurs when a disease is detected by a screening test earlier than it would have been if it were
  • diagnosed by its clinical appearance; time lag of asymptomatic disease is not considered during survival analysis
  • Length bias: an overestimation of survival duration among screened groups due to the disproportionate identification of asymptomatically slowly progressing cases, while fast progressing cases are detected after giving symptoms
  • Will these results help me care for my patients? – consider inclusion/exclusion criteria, result similarity/differences for specific subgroups, whether the technology of interest has changed since the study was published

blocks.html: Definition of a Mental Disorder

• Mental disorder: a syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in an individual’s cognition, emotion regulation, or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning – key is the duration of symptoms and the level of interference/distress in social, occupational, or other activities
  • An expectable, or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss is NOT a mental disorder
  • Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) and conflicts that are primarily between the individual and society are NOT mental disorders UNLESS the deviance or conflict results from a dysfunction in the individual

• Motor cortex in the frontal lobe plans movement on the contralateral side of the brain to the eventual movement
  • Motor neuron axons descend through white matter tracts (internal capsule) → brainstem → decussate in the pyramids of the medulla → descend in spinal cord → VGH → spinal nerve → peripheral nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle

• Pharmacology: field of science concerned with the biology, chemistry, and physiology of drug disposition, effects, and toxicity
  • Drug: a medicine or other substance which has a physiological effect when introduced into the body; used in the diagnosis, treatment, or prevention of a disease or as a component of a medication
  • Clinical pharmacology: the study of drug action in man, providing the scientific basis for rational, safe, and effective prescribing
  • Therapeutics: field of medicine concerned with the use of treatments to cure, control, or prevent disease
  • Prescribing: a written order, which includes detailed instructions of what medicine should be given to whom, in what formulation and dose, by what route, when, how frequently, and for how long
  • Pharmacodynamics: the effects of a drug on the body; how drugs work
  • Pharmacokinetics: the quantitative description of drug concentrations in the body over time; how the body deals with drugs

  • D-R interaction – quantitative relation between dose and effect; selectivity of drug action Orthosteric site = main binding site of the agonist; allosteric sites = other binding sites

Potency and Efficacy of Drugs

• Efficacy (Emax): the maximal response produced by a drug As receptors become occupied, there is an increase in response up to Emax
  • Emax may occur when all receptors are bound or only a fraction are occupied
  • Potency (EC50/ED50): concentration of dose required to produce 50% of the Emax
  • Lower EC50 = more potent drug
  • Competitive antagonists decrease the potency of agonists, but do not change the efficacy
  • Non-competitive antagonists decrease the efficacy of agonists, but do not change the potency
Drug Absorption

• Absorption: the movement of a drug from its site of administration to the systemic circulation Rate of absorption affects onset of action – physiochemical properties/formulations (dissolution, pH, lipid solubility),
  • blood flow, activity of drug transport proteins (OATs, P-glycoprotein), route of administration (therapeutic goal)
  • Amount of drug absorbed determines magnitude of effect
  • Bioavailability: the proportion of administered drug (parent drug) that reaches the systemic circulation in an unaltered form
  • Consider absorption (intrinsic properties of the drug, DDI, DFI) and first-pass metabolism effect

Drug Distribution

• Distribution: the movement of a drug from the main circulation into its sites of action
  • Medication is first carried to highly vascularized tissues – brain, heart, liver, kidneys → skin, muscle, fat, bone
  • Blood brain barrier (BBB): a highly selective semipermeable barrier between the blood circulation and the brain/extracellular fluid around the brain that restricts access of many molecules to the brain – carrier-mediated transport, lipid-soluble substances
  • Volume of distribution (Vd): the extent to which a drug partitions between the plasma and tissue compartments
  • Factors that affect distribution: blood flow, capillary permeability, lipid solubility, disease state (heart/liver/kidney failure), age (↑ body fat, ↓ plasma volume, ↓ total body water, ↓ extracellular body fluid)
Drug Metabolism

• Metabolism: the chemical modification of a drug by a biological system
  • Sites of metabolism: liver (primary site), intestine (enterocytes), stomach (alcohol), kidney, intestinal bacterial
  • Metabolism can activate drugs (prodrug), inactivate drugs, increase/decrease toxicity, increase drug effectiveness

• Phase I – Cytochrome P450 system mediates most oxidation/reduction reactions; exhibit significant genetic variability CYP3A4/5 = 30.2%; CYP2D6 = 20%; CYP2C9 = 12.8%; CYP1A2 = 8.9%
  • Phase II – transferases add hydrophilic groups; glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation, glutathione/thiol combination
  • Enzyme induction = LOWER drug levels; enzyme inhibition = HIGHER drug levels; opposite for prodrugs
  • Increased metabolic rate decreases drug duration/intensity; decreased metabolic rate increases drug duration/intensity
  • Factors that affect metabolism: DDI (enzyme induction/inhibition), disease state (liver/kidney disease, infection, inflammatory disease), age, gender, genetic polymorphisms, blood flow
Drug Excretion

• Excretion: the process of eliminating the parent drug and its metabolites from the body
  • 1. Renal drug excretion: glomerular filtration → passive tubular reabsorption → active tubular secretion → excretion
  • 2. Hepatic metabolism – CYP enzymes
  • 3. Biliary excretion: liver → gallbladder → bile duct → duodenum → excretion in feces OR deconjugated and reabsorbed via hepatic portal vein (enterohepatic recycling); high molecular weight, conjugated drugs, amphipathic molecules
  • Other routes of excretion: lungs (respiration), hair follicles (sweat), salivary glands, breast milk
  • Clearance (CL): rate at which a drug is removed from plasma divided by the concentration of that drug in the plasma (mL/min)
  • Factors that affect excretion: drug related factors (water soluble), blood flow, renal function (GFR), hepatic function, disease state, age (↓ renal plasma flow, ↓ glomerular filtration rate, ↓ number of functional glomeruli)
Clinical Pharmacology

• Graded dose-response curve = one patient
  • Quantal dose-response curve = population of patients; all/none; therapeutic effect (ED50), toxic effect (TD50), lethal effect (LD50)
  • Can extract the % of individuals who exhibit the effect plotted as a function of log dose; standard dose = starting point
  • Half-life (t1/2): the time for the blood concentration of a drug to decline by one-half; dose is usually removed after 3-5 half-lives
  • Determines the duration of drug action and the frequency a drug needs to be given to maintain drug effects
  • Larger volume of distribution = longer t1/2; higher clearance = shorter t1/2; independent of dose
  • Steady state concentration (Css): the plasma drug concentration at which the rate of drug delivery equals the rate of elimination
  • Takes 3-5 half-lives for most drugs to reach the steady-state; independent of dose For every dosing regimen with the same daily dose rate, Css is the same, but the peak and trough fluctuation is different
  • Maintenance dose: maintains a peak plasma concentration below the toxic concentration and a trough plasma concentration above the minimally effective dose
  • Loading dose: larger than the maintenance dose and allows for attainment of therapeutic concentrations more rapidly
  • Therapeutic window: represents the range between the minimum toxic dose and the minimum therapeutic/effective dose
  • ED50 – monitor for efficacy and adverse drug reactions; use as a starting dose when there is a wide therapeutic window; titrate dose when there is a narrow therapeutic window Dosing regimens should be designed to avoid toxicity or lack of efficacy and when possible, to provide convenient

• Adverse drug reaction (ADR): any noxious, unintended, and undesired effect of a drug, which occurs at doses used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy; something bad happens even though you give the right drug, right dose, and right route

rows:

PK interactions involve changes in the disposition of a drug

Alteration in drug elimination is the most common cause of adverse drug interaction
PD interactions involve drugs with complementary or antagonistic therapeutic effects

• Indication: a disorder for which a drug is effective and should be used
  • Contraindication: a disorder for which a drug is harmful and should not be used

blocks.html: Therapeutics in Older Adults

• Polypharmacy: the use of multiple medications by a patient; minimum 5-10 medications
  • Increase in medication = increase in cost, ADRs, poor adherence, DDIs, risk of hospitalization
  • Factors leading to ADRs: multimorbidity, changes in PK/PD with aging, prescribing cascades, heterogeneity, lack of inclusion in clinical research, fragmentation/specialization of healthcare, frequent transitions in care, advances in healthcare/guidelines
  • Review medications at least annually – have patients bring in bottles, at transitions of care, ask about side effects/benefits, look for duplication/cascades, eliminate unnecessary medications, simplify dosing regimens
  • When starting a new medication: Is this medication necessary? Does it align with the patient’s frailty status and goals? Is the medication covered by Ontario Drug Benefits? What are the therapeutic endpoints? Do the benefits outweigh the risks? Are you treating effects of another drug? Could one drug be used to treat two conditions? Could it interact with diseases or other drugs? Does the patient know what it’s for and what to watch out for?

blocks.html: Canadian Health Care System and Drug Therapy

• Health care was designated to be a provincial responsibility at the time of Confederation (not costly, few drugs), but over time, it has expanded to include universal coverage of basic health services and hospital care (40-50% of provincial budgets)
  • 10 provincial systems, 3 territorial systems, small federal system (Canadian Armed Forces, Her Majesty’s prisons)

• Drugs are prescribed by physicians (provincial); paid for by patients/private plans/governments (federal, provincial); approved, regulated, and monitored by the federal government; and sold by industry (federal regulation, provincial incorporation)
  • Drug formulary: a list of medications that are approved for use in a hospital or that are provided by a drug plan
  • All provinces and territories have drug plans – number/type of drugs and eligibility varies considerably
Drug Utilization in Canada

• Total spending on drugs in Canada is $40 billion/year – 16% of health care costs; $1100/person; 85% on prescription drugs
  • 50% of drug costs are paid by public expenditure, 25% by private drug plans, and 25% by individuals
  • Patients ≤ 18 on average receive 4 prescriptions/year; number of drugs prescribed increases with age
  • Top drug classes prescribed: cardiovascular, psychotherapeutics, gastrointestinal/genitourinary
  • Percentage of drug sales: antineoplastic and immunomodulating agents, general anti-infectives, alimentary tract/metabolism
  • Major cost drivers are age high-cost drugs (rheumatoid arthritis/Chron’s disease, Hepatitis C, age-related macular degeneration)
  • OECD average pharmaceutical spending = $719/year per capita; Canada = $1043/year and ranks #3 after USA and Switzerland
  • OCED average life expectancy = 80.6 years; Canada = 81.7, but ranks #13
  • Barriers to optimal drug therapy: finances, SDH, geography, health care system challenges/accessibility
Drug Development and Regulation

• Drugs are approved for sale in Canada by the Health Products and Food Branch of Health Canada
  • Therapeutics Product Directorate – drugs
  • Biologic and Genetic Therapies Directorate – vaccines, biologics
